paragraphs: A Pacific type locomotive is all machinery on display. The boiler sits high, the driving wheels are tall enough to see through, and the running gear - rods, valve gear, crossheads - is out in the open where it can be watched moving. That visibility is why steam locomotives photograph so well and why they are so unforgiving to model.
The mesh runs 696,167 polygons and 367,422 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the rods, the plumbing along the boiler and the cab fittings.

This page carries rigged builds at $169, including versions prepared for Cinema 4D and for Maya, which are the ones to take if the wheels and valve gear have to turn. Aimed at rail heritage and museum work, period film and television, simulators and games. Built to CheckMate specification, on sale since 2024.

A tradesman figure has to look like someone who works rather than someone dressed as a worker. Overalls sit differently from casual trousers, the apron or bib pulls at the shoulders, and the sleeves are usually pushed back. Those small details are what let a figure stand in a workshop scene without looking like a mannequin in costume.

The mesh is light at 13,818 polygons and 14,414 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 20 texture maps at a mix of sizes up to 4096x4096 carrying the fabric weave, the wear and the skin detail.

At $149 and built to StemCell specification, it suits workshop and trades visualisation, vocational education and recruitment material, tool and equipment advertising, architectural scenes needing people, and games. On sale since 2020.

Grid scale storage looks like a shipping container yard because that is essentially what it is: rows of containerised battery units with cooling equipment on the sides, inverters and transformers at the end of each row, and cable trays running between them. That repetition is the whole visual, and it is what makes the scale of a site readable.

The mesh is efficient at 177,873 polygons and 240,846 vertices in quads and tris. The UVs overlap, which is exactly right for a site built from identical units, and it keeps a whole installation affordable in a scene.

At $139 and built to StemCell specification, it suits renewable energy and grid visualisation, utility and infrastructure presentation, investor and trade material, planning documents and games. On sale since 2023.

A combine does three jobs in one pass: cuts, threshes and separates. That is why the machine looks the way it does - a wide header at the front, a body full of drums and sieves, a grain tank on top and an unloading auger swinging out to the side. Being generic rather than branded makes it usable where a manufacturer's badge would be a problem.

The mesh is heavy at 1,257,805 polygons and 646,664 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 21 texture maps at 4096x4096, carrying the paint, the dust and the chaff staining that agricultural machinery always wears.
At $139 it suits agriculture and agritech visualisation, food supply chain presentation, rural landscape scenes, equipment advertising, education material and games. On sale since 2022.

The short range member of this air defence family sits on a lighter chassis than its longer ranged sibling, which changes the whole vehicle: fewer canisters, a smaller erecting frame and a truck that can go places a heavy launcher cannot. The trade is reach for mobility, and that is visible at a glance.

The mesh runs 400,334 polygons and 418,628 vertices with mixed UV layout. The build is described as simplified, which refers to the interior of the cab rather than the launcher itself, and that is the right saving on a vehicle almost always shown from outside.
At $139 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits defence and air defence visualisation, news and documentary graphics, procurement and training presentation, and games. On sale since 2026.

paragraphs: Moving a pot of molten slag is one of the more alarming jobs in heavy industry, and the vehicle built for it reflects that: a low straddle frame that lets the pot ride close to the ground, dozens of small wheels spreading a colossal load, heat shielding along the frame and a cradle that tips the pot to empty it.
The mesh runs 892,066 polygons and 467,708 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the wheel stations, the frame and the cradle mechanism.

At $139 and built to StemCell specification, it suits steel and heavy industry visualisation, plant and logistics presentation, equipment marketing, safety and training material, and games. On sale since 2024.

A puppy following a scent is a very specific animation: nose down, tail up and swinging, the whole body pulled forward by the head while the back legs hurry to keep up. Getting that read requires a rig that lets the spine bend properly and a cycle built around the head rather than the feet, and this build arrives rigged and animated in exactly that motion.
The mesh is light at 23,108 polygons and 23,117 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which keeps the animal usable in real time as well as in an offline render.

A version with fur grooming sits on this page at $169. This build at $139 covers pet and veterinary advertising, family and lifestyle material, children's content, animation and games. Built to CheckMate specification, on sale since 2025.

A sprint car is the most extreme looking thing in circle racing: an enormous wing on the roof, another over the nose, a tube frame with almost no bodywork and wheels of different sizes on each corner to help it turn left on dirt. Nothing about it is subtle, and nothing about it is optional.

The mesh runs 816,842 polygons and 855,625 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the tube frame, the suspension linkages and the wing structures where the machine is examined.
At $129 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits motorsport visualisation and broadcast graphics, racing advertising, dirt track and speedway scenes, racing games and print. On sale since 2024.

A disassembled phone only works as an asset if the parts are genuinely separate objects that could go back together. Display assembly, battery, logic board, camera module, speakers, shields and screws all exist here as their own bodies, so the layout can be exploded along an axis, laid flat for a teardown spread or animated back into the chassis.
The mesh runs 220,105 polygons and 236,444 vertices in quads and tris with mixed UV layout, with the detail concentrated in the connector housings and the camera assembly where a macro camera lands.

At $129 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits repair and service documentation, technology journalism and teardown content, product and engineering marketing, teaching material and games. On sale since 2026.

The 717 is a rear-engined twin with a T-tail, which puts it in a different visual family from every other Boeing airliner flying. Short, high-tailed and with its engines mounted on the fuselage rather than the wings, it is instantly recognisable on a regional apron - and Delta operated more of them than anyone.
The mesh is efficient at 121,423 polygons and 133,836 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which suits an aircraft usually shown at an airport rather than in extreme close-up.
At $129 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits airline marketing, regional airport visualisation, aviation journalism and archive material, film and television, and games. On sale since 2025.

The 777-300 is one of the longest airliners ever built, and length is the first thing to get right: the fuselage runs so far behind the wing that the aircraft needs a tail strike protection system on rotation. In Emirates colours it carries the red tail and the gold script that have to follow a very long curved surface without distortion.

The mesh runs 754,269 polygons and 774,167 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 12 texture maps - 6 at 8192x8192 and 6 at 4096x4096. Six maps at the largest size is what a fuselage this long needs to avoid visible repetition.
A rigged build sits on this page at $149. The static model at $129 covers airline marketing, airport visualisation, film and television, news graphics and print. On sale since 2016.

Putting a light aircraft on floats changes it more than it first appears. The aeroplane sits far higher, the floats add their own struts and water rudders, and the whole machine gains a nose-up attitude on the water that it never has on wheels. This build carries the float structure, the spreader bars and the rigging.

The mesh runs 526,555 polygons and 551,931 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 15 texture maps - 8 at 8192x8192 and 7 at 4096x4096, which is a generous budget for an aircraft this size and shows in the panel and rivet detail.

This page carries five other builds, in red and yellow at $129 and rigged versions at $139. Aimed at bush aviation and wilderness visualisation, lake and coastal scenes, tourism advertising, film and television, and games. On sale since 2016.

A chihuahua is mostly head. The skull is domed and disproportionately large, the eyes are set wide and prominent, the ears stand up like sails and the body behind all that is tiny. Those proportions are the breed, and a scaled-down generic dog reads as a puppy of something else entirely.

The mesh is remarkably light at 7,035 polygons and 6,105 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 11 texture maps at a mix of sizes up to 4096x4096. It arrives rigged, which on an animal this small matters most around the head and neck.

Three more rigged builds share this page at the same $129, prepared for Cinema 4D, Maya and Modo. Aimed at pet advertising, veterinary and animal care material, family and lifestyle imagery, animation and games. Built to CheckMate specification, on sale since 2015.

The Checker was built to be a taxi and nothing else, which is why it looks so unlike a car of its era. Upright glass, a flat roof, enormous rear doors and a body that changed almost not at all across two decades - the design was fixed by what passengers and drivers needed rather than by what was fashionable that year.

The mesh runs 196,808 polygons and 205,150 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the bumpers, the roof light and the door frames that give the car its slab-sided character.

This page carries a second static build at $129 and rigged versions at $149, including builds prepared for Maya and for Cinema 4D. Aimed at period film and television, urban visualisation, advertising, games and print. Built to CheckMate specification, on sale since 2024.
